messages.subject_clean: image cropping based on spatial positioning
messages.body_plain:
Hi Filipe,

Good to hear you have plans to improve this aspect of FIELDimageR, I will look forward to testing the modifications when available. Until then, I will test the suggestions you provided. I am currently pushing the recommended maximum mosaic size, so it may be best for me to crop images prior to FIELDimageR processing, just to keep the input mosaic file size as low as possible.

Thanks again,
Brian

On Saturday, February 26, 2022 at 1:20:48 PM UTC-5 fmatias wrote:
>
> Hi Brian,
>
>
>
> Thanks for sharing your experience and thoughts with us. For the next version of FIELDimageR, I have some ideas to improve this step… I will let you know when it is done.
>
>
>
> In the meantime, there are some great solutions. Do you know the package UAStools (https://github.com/andersst91/UAStools)? This package allows using only the coordinate information from each corner to build the plot shapefile, check this tutorial from Steven L. Anderson https://github.com/andersst91/UAStools/wiki/plotshpcreate.R. Also, there is a great workshop video that combines UAStools and FIELDimageR presented by Alper Adak. Here is the link https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=O-xmC8qCt7k.
>
>
>
> Another possibility is to use QGIS to build your plot shapefile. Here is a great workshop presented by Diego Gris https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wrPPKSniXW0.
>
>
>
> In case you have experience with python, Tyler Nigon presented this super cool tool to make plot shapefiles as well. Check this workshop link https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=k26YPRY4qdk
>
>
>
> Hope one of these solutions helps you… Please, let us know if it works.
>
>
>
> All the best,
>
> Filipe
>
> Em quarta-feira, 23 de fevereiro de 2022 às 17:42:43 UTC-3, Brian Abernathy escreveu:
> > Hello,
> >
> > I have a situation that is a bit different from the tutorial examples. The field I'm working on has several thousand ~1m x 1m research plots. This makes any FIELDimageR functions that require manual selection, like fieldShape(), difficult to perform precisely due to the small image window and inability to zoom in rstudio.
> >
> > My current workaround is to use an image editor (gimp) to rotate and crop my raw images while zoomed in to precisely select the field corners. These rotated/cropped images can then be processed automatically using the fieldShape() extent = TRUE option. (instructs fieldShape() to use the entire image and skip manual corner selection) This works well for basic processing like canopy percentage. However, gimp is not geotiff-aware, so it does not export spatial information after rotating/cropping, crippling it's usefulness.
> >
> > Moving forward, I'm considering pre-processing steps similar to those above. Avoiding manual selections in FIELDimageR while retaining spatial information in the rotated/cropped TIFs is the goal. Ideally I'd automate as much of the processing as possible for consistency (and speed!) between the time-series images I have. This seems feasible, but I have very limited experience with geotiff files and am not sure if there is a way to get spatial coordinates from field corners in an image and if those coordinates can be used for cropping. If anyone has experience doing this, I'd like to hear more about your process.
> >
> > Thanks,
> > Brian

> > > > On Monday, February 14, 2022 at 9:46:41 AM UTC-5 foreste...@gmail.com wrote:
> > > > > Hi Brian,
> > > > >
> > > > > This is true and we always have differences between lighting conditions. I normalized each RGB image using the mean and standard deviation (some author using mean and standard deviation between all the images too):
> > > > >
> > > > > # Normalized values in RGB --------------------------------------------------------
> > > > > library(terra)
> > > > > RGB<- terra::rast("YOUR_IMAGE.tif")
> > > > > RGB <- subset(RGB, 1:3)
> > > > > norf <- function(x, ...) {
> > > > >   v <- values(x)
> > > > >   v <- (v - mean(v)) / sd(v)
> > > > >   setValues(x, (255 / (max(v)-min(v))) * (v-min(v)))
> > > > > }
> > > > >
> > > > > # `sapp` loops over layers
> > > > > RGB.normalized <- sapp(RGB, norf)
> > > > >
> > > > > The reference paper is (Page 6):
> > > > >
> > > > > Xu, D.; Pu, Y.; Guo, X. A Semi-Automated Method to Extract Green and Non-Photosynthetic Vegetation Cover from RGB Images in Mixed Grasslands. Sensors 2020, 20, 6870. https://doi.org/10.3390/s20236870
> > > > >
> > > > > Cheers,
> > > > >
> > > > > Alexandre
> > > > >

> > > > > >
> > > > > > While my results are useful, I've been looking for ways to improve them. My images are a time-series set of field plots taken every 2 weeks. I've noticed some unexpected variation between some sets and have considered that this variation could be due to differences between lighting conditions when the images were captured. Some of the mosaics appear clear and bright while others appear to have some (cloud?) shading.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Is it recommended to normalize sets of images to minimize differences in brightness prior to FIELDimageR processing? If so, can you recommend any specific tools or protocols to use/follow?
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Thanks,
> > > > > > Brian

On Saturday, February 26, 2022 at 7:03:57 PM UTC-5 foreste...@gmail.com wrote:
> Hi Brian,
>
> Just as another tip. Despite this empirical approach solving almost
> all cases is possible to obtain a thresholding value by some criteria
> decision like Otsu’s multilevel thresholding method (MOM). The
> autothresholdr package does it, but index values must be discretized.
> For example for an NDVI raster:
>
> land_ndvi_F <- round(land_ndvi*100,0)
>
> # Percentile Otsu’s multilevel thresholding method (MOM)
> MOM<-auto_thresh(
> int_arr=values(land_ndvi_F),
> method="Percentile",
> ignore_black = FALSE,
> ignore_white = FALSE,
> ignore_na = TRUE
> )
> MOM
> [1] 33
> or 0.33 in real NDVI data scale.
>
> Best wishes,
> Alexandre
>
>
> Em sáb., 26 de fev. de 2022 às 14:34, fmatias
> <filipem...@gmail.com> escreveu:
> >
> > Hi Brian,
> >
> >
> >
> > Thanks for asking us. The best way is to choose different vegetation indices and try to find the best thresholding value to make your segmentation between plants and soil. Please, check this example using the index “BGI”: https://github.com/OpenDroneMap/FIELDimageR#P6. Normally, plotting the histogram helps to find the best clipping point (between pics of histogram bars)
> >
> >
> >
> > Image<- stack("Image.tif")
> >
> > Image.BGI<- fieldIndex(mosaic = Image, index = c("BGI"))
> >
> > dev.off()
> >
> > hist(Image.BGI$BGI) # Image segmentation start from 0.7 (soil and plants)
> >
> > EX1.BGI<- fieldMask(mosaic = EX1.Rotated, Red = 1, Green = 2, Blue = 3,
> >
> > index = "BGI", cropValue = 0.7, cropAbove = T)
> >
> > #Check if: cropValue=0.8 or cropValue=0.6 works better.
> >
> >
> >
> >
> > Also, there are some explanation about image segmentation in this tutorial of how to count seeds from images using FIELDimagR. Besides being different objects (seeds vs. plants) the idea to segment the background is the same You can use this to understand the concepts. Here is the link https://filipematias23.github.io/FIELDimageR-Workshop-12/#example-03
> >
> >
> >
> >
> > Hope it helps,
> >
> > Filipe
> >
